what: The score is the negative saving obtained by inserting the customer instead of serving it on a singleton depot-customer-depot route. That saving is divided by 1 + demand/remaining_capacity, a bounded capacity-pressure factor in [1, 2]. Thus lower scores favor large geometric savings while mildly preferring candidates that consume less of the current route's scarce residual capacity. It uses the caller-fixed insertion edge and costs O(len(route)) time and O(1) space.
why: The identity between singleton-route cost 2*d(depot, customer) and insertion cost gives a natural route-merging surrogate: it rewards customers whose inclusion most reduces depot travel, rather than merely choosing the smallest raw detour. This is useful when fleet size is unrestricted because avoidable depot legs directly affect total distance. The mild capacity adjustment addresses the strongly heterogeneous demands visible in the representative instances without allowing demand to overwhelm geometry; its effect is bounded by a factor of two. The rule is still greedy: it does not predict later insertions, route closures, RCL randomness, or the exact result of 2-opt, and no empirical improvement is claimed.
